candidates.raw_excerpt: As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. candidates.title: Double asteroid solar eclipse caught on camera | Space photo of the day for Nov. 24, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: (Image credit: ESA) A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another. What is it? The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system , which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos. The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Didymos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its trajectory. Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. Why is it incredible? For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth. But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid , meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet. Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

China's Xizang Autonomous Region switched on the first turbines of its biggest wind farm on Monday, sending power from the 5,100-meter-high Himalayas into the regional grid before winter.

The new power units are part of the 150-megawatt phase-one project at the Qiongjie wind base in Shannan City, southern Xizang. After its completion, the base is expected to produce 394 million kilowatt-hour a year – power for roughly 175,000 households and about 330,000 tonnes of avoided CO2 emissions. It will also back up the grid during nighttime, when solar output falls to zero, and in the winter, when hydropower is low.

Phase one will see the installation of 24 turbines, each rated at 6.25 MW, on ridges averaging 5,100 meters above sea level, where average wind speeds exceed 8 meters per second. Tower sections weigh up to 101.9 tonnes, blades measure 97.3 meters in length, and the hubs are positioned 113 meters above the ground.

candidates.title: Sleeping at wheel: China draws the line as self-driving rules tighten
candidates.raw_excerpt:
A car drove itself over 5 kilometers before dawn, with a drunk driver asleep in the back seat. It stopped automatically and bystanders called the police. On Monday, a court in east China's Hangzhou sentenced the driver, surnamed Mao, to detention and a fine for drunk driving.

His blood-alcohol level was 169 milligrams per 100 milliliters, against the 80 mg/ml threshold. He had set a route home and activated assisted driving rather than call a designated driver, then moved to the rear seat for a sleep.

An official notice disclosed neither the vehicle's brand nor its driver-assistance system.

What matters is the car's action next: having lost the takeover signal, the system triggered its safety fallback and stopped. Monitoring the driver, degrading to a minimal-risk maneuver and leaving data for investigators are what China's new mandatory standards require.

China classifies autonomous driving using the scale of the Society of Automotive Engineers: Level 2 (L2) keeps the driver responsible throughout, L3 lets the system drive within a defined area, and L4 needs no driver.

Two standards are coming. GB 47955-2026, covering L2 combined driver assistance, takes effect on January 1, 2027. GB 44721-2026, the first mandatory national standard for L3 and L4 systems, follows on July 1, 2027. It requires takeover-capability monitoring for L3, mandates a minimal-risk maneuver that pulls over rather than stops in a live lane, and makes event-data recording compulsory.

China is set to break its longest spaceflight record, allowing astronaut Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 mission crew, to spend a full year in orbit, the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) announced on Tuesday.

Zhu will remain aboard the China Space Station through the Shenzhou-24 crew rotation. Both missions are scheduled to last six months.

"This is by no means a simple accumulation of two six-month missions," CMSA spokesperson Zhang Jingbo said at a press conference at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China.

Zhang said the year-long stay is designed to pursue two objectives: establishing a new human space research system to study how the body adapts to and changes under spaceflight conditions, and systematically validating the station's capacity to support an astronaut's health, work and daily life over an extended period.

A stress test

Bone loss alone proceeds at 1% to 2% per month in microgravity. Even with roughly two hours of daily exercise aboard the International Space Station (ISS), astronauts can still lose significant muscle mass during shorter missions. A continuous year in orbit eliminates the physiological "reset" that occurs when astronauts return to Earth between separate flights, allowing researchers to observe whether these changes plateau, worsen or trigger new adaptation mechanisms.

candidates.title: China, Pakistan to conduct cooperative space station experiments
candidates.raw_excerpt:
China and Pakistan will conduct four cooperative scientific experiments aboard China Space Station, involving cyanobacteria, quinoa seeds and two types of composite materials, according to  the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The Pakistani astronaut on a short-term flight on China Space Station will carry out related experimental operations in orbit.

One of the experiments, proposed by Pakistan’s Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission, will examine how cyanobacteria grow and absorb carbon dioxide in space, providing data for future oxygen regeneration and biological production. Cyanobacteria are tiny organisms that use sunlight to grow and release oxygen. The organisms used in the experiment come from Pakistan.

Another experiment, led by the University of Agriculture Faisalabad, will expose 32 quinoa seed samples to the space environment to study their resilience and longevity.

Two materials experiments will test the protective performance of graphene-based composites and the repair efficiency of self-healing carbon fiber composites.

The Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who will take a short-term flight on China Space Station, will carry out related experimental operations in orbit, according to Chen Mengyun, International Cooperation Project Manager at the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Chinese and Pakistani scientific teams will also jointly publish papers and share the results of the experiments, said Chen.

The space station will continue to solicit, select and implement new space science projects, Chen said.

She added that China Space Station, also the national space laboratory, is open to scientists worldwide. It solicits proposals for space science and application projects from global scientists on an ongoing basis each year.

To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. The Earth system intelligence research platform "ZHU·GE" was launched on Monday at the 2026 Xiongan International Symposium on Meteorological Artificial Intelligence.

The name ZHU·GE is derived from the initials of "Zone-to-global Holistic Understanding by Generative Earth-system modeling," reflecting its goal of enabling understanding across scales, from local to global, and advancing from observational facts to scientific understanding.

Aimed at advancing AI for Science (AI4S) in Earth sciences, the platform can turn research ideas into verifiable scientific findings by drawing on vast amounts of data. It is designed to help translate scientific understanding into operational capabilities.

After researchers submit their research objectives in natural language, the platform can independently search and access relevant literature, data and model resources, devise research approaches, write code, conduct experiments and analyze results. It can also dynamically adjust its research direction based on feedback. Its applications include research into scientific mechanisms, development of forecasting methods, scientific modeling and model optimization.
